Subject: Tool-calling integration patterns — follow-up & post-call recap

Alex — great to meet earlier. Quick recap of the call and proposed next steps so we have a single source of truth. TL;DR: Redwood can support FinApps' intended architecture (server-side SDK + routing layer + embeddings re-ranker) with several common tool-calling patterns; next step is a 60-min technical deep-dive with FinApps engs to confirm auth and routing details.

What we covered (high level):
- SDK setup: use Redwood server SDK (Python/Node) for request proxying and typed tool definitions. We recommend server-side usage to keep keys and tool credentials private.
- Auth: two options discussed — API-key with short TTL + signer for sensitive ops, or mTLS for high-security customers. We can support both; mTLS requires additional network config on Private/Dedicated.
- Routing & model variants: route by policy (latency/cost/region). For FinApps, suggested primary route = rwd-gpt-embed-1 for embeddings + rwd-chat-tooling-1 for generation; fallback to smaller quantized variants when capacity constrained.
- Structured output & tool calling: define explicit tool schemas (name, inputs, outputs, error model). Use Redwood's structured-output enforcement for higher recall on critical ops.
- Embeddings + reranker pattern: generate top-K candidates via semantic search, score with a lightweight reranker (embedding dot + shallow model), then use tool call to execute actions (e.g., retrieve ledger row, run reconciliation).
- Parallel tools/async calls: for independent tools, run in parallel with an aggregator step; for dependent flows, chain calls with strict timeout/error semantics.
- Error handling: surface partial failures back to app with error codes, implement retry/backoff for idempotent ops, and fail-open policies for non-critical tooling.

Action items / next steps (owner):
- Marissa: share a focused SDK integration snippet + example tool definitions (attached).
- Dev: schedule 60-min technical deep-dive with FinApps eng (proposed times below).
- Alex/FinApps: confirm preferred auth approach (API-key vs mTLS) and whether you want embeddings + reranker in scope for initial POC.

Proposed times for deep-dive (PT): Thurs 2/19 9:00-10:00, 11:00-12:00 or Fri 2/20 8:00-9:00. Let us know what works and we’ll send a calendar invite.

Attached: redwood-sdk-integration-snippet.py (quickstart), finapps-tool-definitions-example.json (example tool schemas), rdw-tool-calling-patterns-one-pager.pdf

Perfect — adding Priya and Nikhil here. Confirmed: Thurs 2/19 11:00-12:00 PT. Invite will follow.

Answers to Alex's questions:
1) Incremental auth rollout: yes — you can start with API-key in staging and migrate to mTLS for prod without changing tool definitions. Tool schemas remain stable; the transport/auth layer swaps out at the SDK/proxy layer. We usually version auth configs separately from tool definitions (example attached in the snippet).

2) Parallel tools / SDK concerns: the Redwood server SDK supports async parallel tool invocation and exposes a connection-pool config. Best practices:
   - Use a pool size matched to your concurrency; default pool settings are conservative.
   - Set per-tool timeouts and an overall aggregate timeout. If one tool is non-critical, set a short soft timeout and continue with partial results.
   - Monitor tail latency — parallel calls amplify tail risks; enable traced sampling in the SDK to see slow callers.

3) Cost estimate (rough): example flow you mentioned:
   - Retrieve top-200 candidates (embedding search): ~200 embedding vector ops + 200 DB reads.
   - Rerank top-20 (embed dot + small model): ~20 model calls (we recommend a small reranker model or a light-weight MLP scoring function).
   - Final generation for answer: 1 generation request (size depends on max tokens).
   Ballpark: for your workload we estimate ~0.6–1.2 embedding units per query and 0.2–0.6 generation units; we'll provide a more precise estimate after we see sample QPS and average doc sizes.

Attached: redwood-sdk-integration-snippet.py (contains an example auth-switch pattern, parallel tool helper, and a sample tool definition for the ledger lookup). Also attached a sample finapps-tool-definitions-example.json and a one-pager on patterns.
